name: Erythropoietin

lead: Erythropoietin (EPO) is the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. Injectable versions treat anaemia in kidney disease and chemotherapy patients, and some physique users discuss it for stamina and recovery capacity in training.

It binds the EPO receptor on red-cell precursors, activating JAK2 signalling to increase red blood cell production and oxygen-carrying capacity. It is known mostly as an endurance-sport doping agent; clinical trials reviewed were in anaemic patients, and none aimed at appearance.

paras: Medically it is prescribed as an injectable for anaemia. In endurance sport it has been used to raise red cell mass, and in physique circles it is mentioned as a way to train harder and longer.
It is a prescription-only drug. Reported risks in patients include serious cardiovascular events and increased mortality in some groups, and it is banned in competitive sport.

angle.text: Erythropoietin raises red blood cell count, increasing oxygen delivery so users can train harder and longer, which some physique users link to more muscle and leanness. Its performance effects are studied in endurance athletes; a direct effect on muscle or appearance has not been tested.

lead: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone made mainly by the kidneys in response to low oxygen; it stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. Its gene is switched on by hypoxia-inducible factors, and it signals through the EPO receptor and JAK2 [1][2][3][4].

Recombinant human EPO (epoetin alfa, first approved by the US FDA in 1989 according to Grokipedia) is used to treat anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia [4]. In sport and fitness communities it is known as an endurance-boosting performance drug because raising red cell mass increases oxygen-carrying capacity. Its connection to appearance runs via the muscle and body-composition culture in which it is sometimes mentioned.

Beyond erythropoiesis, laboratory research has examined EPO as a neuroprotective agent, reporting that it crosses the blood-brain barrier in animals and reduces ischaemic brain injury [5][6][7]. Grokipedia notes that medical use has raised safety concerns, including increased mortality and serious cardiovascular events in some patient groups [4].
infobox: Epoetin alfa, epoetin beta and others
Anaemia of kidney disease and chemotherapy

paras: EPO binds its receptor on erythroid progenitor cells, which lack their own kinase domain; binding triggers phosphorylation and activation of JAK2, driving survival, proliferation and maturation [3][4]. Production is regulated by oxygen: under hypoxia the transcription factor HIF-1 binds an enhancer of the EPO gene, and HIF-1 was found to be a general mediator of hypoxic transcription in many cell types [1][2][8]. HIF-2 alpha is described as the dominant isoform in kidney EPO production [4].

Animal studies reported that systemically given recombinant EPO reduced focal ischaemic brain injury and that EPO receptors are present at brain capillaries [5][7]. Other work reported anti-apoptotic signalling involving Jak2 and NF-kappaB [9][6]. A 2002 paper reported that EPO therapy for acute stroke was safe and beneficial [10].

Registered clinical trials of EPO products are largely in anaemia. They include phase 3 comparisons of biosimilar epoetin alfa with the reference product in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients [11][12][13], long-term safety studies of a further epoetin [14][15], and trials of epoetin in leukemia and chemotherapy-related anaemia [16][17][18]. A phase 2 study begun in 1993 examined the time course of EPO activity in renal failure [19]. These registrations concern patients with disease; none in the sources reviewed tests EPO for appearance or looksmaxxing goals in healthy people.

Grokipedia reports that medical use of recombinant EPO has been associated with increased mortality, serious cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke, and other risks in some patient populations [4]. The source reviewed gives limited detail, and readers should consult drug labels for authoritative safety information.
EPO is a prescription drug and its use for performance enhancement is prohibited in competitive sport. The sources reviewed contain no documented looksmaxxing-forum discussion of EPO.
